claims.text: Average electron count per atom (e/a) is a primary governor of superconducting behavior in HEAs outside Nb-Ta-dominated and Ti-rich matrices.
The degree of atomic disorder is a primary governor of superconducting behavior in these HEAs.
Increasing e/a while retaining a single-phase solid solution will increase Tc.
Substitution with elements having higher valence-electron numbers will increase the alloy's average e/a.
The proposed comparison will keep every constituent at or above 5 atomic percent while varying e/a.
The proposed alloys will be synthesized at room temperature and characterized for superconductivity below 10 K.
The comparison requires retention of a single-phase solid solution without significant ordering or phase separation.
Higher e/a increases the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
An increased density of states at the Fermi level enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Excessive disorder can suppress superconductivity by localizing electrons.
Phase separation can suppress superconductivity by reducing electronic coherence.
At comparable disorder and with the solid solution retained, higher-e/a alloys will have higher Tc than the lower-e/a baseline.
If phase separation or ordering occurs, Tc will decrease or superconductivity will be suppressed.
The baseline is the initial lower-e/a HEA measured for Tc under conditions identical to those used for the modified alloys.
The hypothesis applies only to single-phase HEAs containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
The hypothesis excludes Nb-Ta-dominated alloys, Ti-rich alloys, and alloys with significant ordering or phase separation.
Failure of Tc to increase with e/a, or a decrease in Tc at higher e/a despite retained single-phase structure and comparable disorder, would falsify the hypothesis.
